truth:
The die plot is not a mirror image of PRM Fig. 1-3 or of the die view.
- Both put the PCIe/I-O pair at the east (right) end of the top row. They differ only in the order of those two cells.
- The die plot (MPR Dec 2020 Fig. 1; the same plot as IEEE Micro 2022 Fig. 7) shows four minion tiles, then the purple Maxion (I/O) box fifth and the orange PCIe box sixth.
- An east-west mirror of the die view would put I/O then PCIe at the west end, in columns 1-2, with memory shires 0-3 on the east.
- The die plot labels no memory shire, so it says nothing about which side memory shires 0-3 are on.

So it is the die view with columns 5 and 6 swapped. L24's own column numbers (5,6 against 6,5) already show a swap, not a mirror (5,6 to 2,1).

truth:
Two errors.
1. The part opens another part's panel: circuitkit.js maps the key 'sync' to the level shifter's panel.
2. A reply's data bits are not re-timed through two flip-flops. They cross into the shire through the VC FIFO: each word is written into the FIFO's storage on the sending clock. where: Die scale, part 'The mesh' (fact list): fact mesh.no-counters; the facts table.
page_said: 'There are no NoC performance counters in the PRM, the firmware or core-et; mesh transit is inferred from latency differences.' (kind spec)
truth:
The firmware's generated NoC register header defines counters in every NoC bridge.
- Each master bridge has two 32-bit counters (*_m_am_cntr0/1, field CNTR) with transaction filters:
  - *_ccmd0/1, with fields TYP, INTFID, VAL, RDY, LOC, PROT, QOS, CACHE, BAR, DOMAIN and SNOOP, and their masks *_ccmdmsk0/1;
  - a capture address and mask (*_caddr/_caddrmsk).
- Each master bridge also has *_latnum0/1.
- Slave bridges have *_s_as_cntr with *_ccmd/_ccmdmsk.
- The bridges exist for the 34 minion shires (NOC_ESR_BRIDGE_ARRAY_COUNT 0x22), the memory shires, PCIe and I/O.

The PRM does not document them and the firmware's code never uses them, but the header defines them. The lab's own 25 Sep lab-problems page asks for 'a way to read the NoC router and bridge counters'.

evidence.quote: /* Register: ns_am_bridge.ns_bridge.bridge_l2tol3b_m_am_cntr0 */ ... bridge_l2tol3b_m_am_cntr1 ... bridge_l3_s_as_cntr

#define NOC_ESR_BRIDGE_ARRAY_COUNT 0x22ull
a way to read the NoC router and bridge counters
There are **no NoC performance counters** in the PRM, the firmware (only FlexNoC address maps in noc_reconfig_memshire.c) or core-et.
Register: ns_am_bridge.ns_bridge.bridge_l2tol3b_m_am_cntr0 ... _m_am_cntr1 ... bridge_l3_s_as_cntr ... NS_BRIDGE_BRIDGE_L2TOL3B_M_AM_CNTR0_CNTR_MSB 31u ... _M_AM_LATNUM0_CNTR_MSB 31u

They sit on the service processor's main-NoC register bus (0x42000000, hal_device.h), which no user kernel reaches.

where: Scale shire.meshstop.xing, 'Voltage and clock crossing (VCFIFO)'. It is reached from the mesh stop's part 'Voltage and clock crossing' and from a minion's ET-Link port ('The crossing into the shire's clock and voltage'). Affected: its drawing and its parts fifo, lvin, ls and sync (screenshot scale-060-shire.meshstop.xing.png).
page_said: Title and blurb: 'Voltage and clock crossing (VCFIFO) ... The shire's cache runs at 0.705 V on its own clock, the network at 0.485 V and 400 MHz.' The drawing under it: 'The crossing · a level shifter / the neighbourhood's bank FIFO is a VC FIFO with level shifters built in (documented); the circuit is generic', with boxes 'neighbourhood (LV)' → 'VC FIFO + level shifters' → 'catch FIFO → bank (HV)' and the rail 'VDDL 0.517 V'. Part sync is 'A two-flip-flop synchroniser in the receiving clock' (FF, FF → 'to the bank', clocked by 'HV clock').
truth:
The title and blurb describe one crossing and the drawing shows another.
- What is drawn is the neighbourhood-to-shire-channel crossing, not the mesh stop's crossing.
- That crossing is semi-synchronous: the neighbourhood clock is the shire clock shifted 180° by the DLL. ET-Link requests and responses pass through semi-synchronous VC FIFOs with a fixed 1.5-cycle hand-off and no synchroniser.
- The two-stage synchronisers belong to the shire cache's VCFIFOs at the NoC. That is the crossing the title and blurb describe (shire clock to the 400 MHz, 0.485 V mesh), and the scale never draws it.

evidence.quote: As the two clocks used in the Neighborhood have the same source, both domains are separated by a semi-synchronous interface (i.e. same clock with a different phase). ... ET-Link request | Output | Semi-synchronous FIFO; ET-Link response | Input | Semi-synchronous FIFO

truth:
The RTL that L103 cites (core-et-main shirecache_mesh_master.sv:141-153) picks the to_l3 lane by the bank the request goes to.

page_said: The shire's cache runs at 0.705 V on its own clock, the network at 0.485 V and 400 MHz. Every bit that crosses is shifted in voltage and re-timed through two flip-flops into the other clock, so it cannot be caught half-changed.
truth:
The blurb is wrong on two points.
- In a VCFIFO only the FIFO's gray-coded write and read counts pass through the two-flip-flop synchronisers. The data words are written into the FIFO's storage in the sending clock and read in the receiving clock once the synchronised count shows them complete. Re-timing each data bit through two flip-flops would let a multi-bit word be caught half-changed.
- Only the SRAM arrays are known to sit on the 0.705 V rail. The page itself says the rail of the cache's logic is not documented ('VDDH (rail asked)'; fact l2.rail.hv-logic).

truth:
The credit counters are not in the UC block.

where: Chip fact minion.one-ready-bit, shown in the facts list of the minion scale's 'Fast local network' (fln) part and on the messaging panels that list it.
page_said: The hardware keeps one peer-to-peer ready bit per minion, not one per partner: a minion receiving from two TensorSend partners at once hangs its hart permanently (the card then needs a reset).
truth: The single bit (partner_ready_peer, 'Peer is ready to receive from me') belongs to the sender. It is read only in the sender-only state Reduce_Wait_Ready. Readies go from a TensorRecv back to its sender. The hazard is a minion that TensorSends to two partners whose readies arrive before it has used the first one: one ready is lost, and that receiver and its sender wait forever. A minion receiving data from two senders posts one ready per TensorRecv, so the bit does not break it. The fact's own source says 'receive readies from two TensorSend partners'; the fact drops 'readies' and so describes the reverse case.

page_said: Each minion has a private 4 KB L1 data cache: 16 sets × 4 ways × 64 B lines, not coherent with any other cache, writing back whole 64-byte lines. [source: ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.1 (slide 2); ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.9 (§2.1.1.5)]
truth: The statement is true, but neither cited page says the L1 writes back whole lines. The slide gives 16 sets, 4 ways, 64 B lines and non-coherent; the datasheet gives the geometry and the LRAM blocks. The Minion DCache Description is the document that says it: an evict is always 512 bits.

evidence.quote: Evict operations (REQ_Write): always 512b in two transfer cycles of 256b each, reading from the LRAM 256b in every cycle. Triggers for these operations are the cacheOps upon a core request or MH when a dirty line has to be replaced.
16-set, 4-way structure with 64 bytes per line. ... The physical data cache memory is organized as 4 LRAM (Latch-RAM) blocks, with 128 rows and 64 bits per row.
L1 Data Cache (L1D$) - 4KB configurable • 16 sets, 4 ways, 64 Bytes cache line • Non-coherent • Configuration through mcache_control CSR
16-set, 4-way structure with 64 bytes per line. ... The physical data cache memory is organized as 4 LRAM (Latch-RAM) blocks, with 128 rows and 64 bits per row.

Evict operations (REQ_Write): always 512b in two transfer cycles of 256b each, reading from the LRAM 256b in every cycle. Triggers for these operations are the cacheOps upon a core request or MH when a dirty line has to be replaced.
Eviction. This operations evicts an individual cache line from a cache, writing it back to the next level of the cache hierarchy if the line is dirty.

truth: A 64-byte line on a x16 BL16 channel takes two 32-byte bursts, so the DRAM chip accounts for about 28 cycles: tRCD 18.2 ns + RL 19.3 ns + 2 × 4.29 ns = 46.1 ns = 27.7 cycles at 600 MHz. The memory shire takes at most ~63 cycles (~105 ns). The cited anatomy page and the architecture notes were corrected to this on 27-28 Sep. The page contradicts itself: its own memory-shire drawing says "the DRAM's own timing: about 28 cycles" and "≤ 63 cycles", and its channel timeline draws two bursts.

page_said: Panel: "Compared with JEDEC LPDDR4 as recalled, not checked against the standard (generic): the timings are close to its limits for this density and rate". Fact: "The programmed timings are close to JEDEC LPDDR4's limits for a 16 Gb-per-channel die at 3,733 MT/s ... tRFCab 280 ns". Note: "tRFCab = 280 ns is the JEDEC value for 12-16 Gb per channel, a cross-check on the die density."
truth: The LPDDR4 refresh table gives tRFCab = 130 ns (2 Gb per channel), 180 ns (3-4 Gb), 280 ns (6-8 Gb) and 380 ns (12-16 Gb). The programmed all-bank refresh (262 DFI clocks = 280.7 ns) is therefore 100 ns under JEDEC's figure for the 16 Gb channel the page asserts (2 GB per channel). Under JEDEC, 280 ns would point to 8 Gb per channel, so it is no cross-check on 16 Gb. It is legal only because Micron rates its 16 Gb single-channel die at an 'improved' 280 ns that supersedes JEDEC. That fits the card's Micron part, but it is a vendor value, not a JEDEC limit.

skeptic: The claim is real. Micron's LPDDR4/4X datasheet reproduces the JEDEC refresh table in Table 111, by density per channel: tRFCab 130 ns (2 Gb), 180 (3-4 Gb), 280 (6-8 Gb), 380 (12-16 Gb). JESD209-4 as I know it says the same. Micron's Table 3 rates its 16 Gb single-channel die at 280 ns as 'improved values from JEDEC'. The card has 2 GB per channel = 16 Gb, so JEDEC asks 380 ns. The programmed t_rfc_min = 0x106 = 262 DFI clocks = 280.7 ns is about 100 ns under that. The page has it wrong in three places: the note ('280 ns is the JEDEC value for 12-16 Gb per channel, a cross-check on the die density', shipped in ladder-img/ladder-data.json), the statement's JEDEC list (tRFCab 280 ns, in the chip facts table) and the tl panel ('close to its limits for this density'). The 'generic, as recalled' caveat does not excuse a wrong generic value, and it sets up a false cross-check. The checker's fix needs four corrections. (a) Changing only the list leaves the statement's lead 'close to JEDEC LPDDR4's limits' contradicted by 280.7 against 380, so the lead must name the exception. (b) The panel's new numbers should come through N rows, not literals: dr_trfc exists, and a new memory-levels N row is needed for 380 ns (the chip build imports any n() key circuitkit.js uses, build_facts.py:1002). (c) 'Fits the card's Micron part' overstates: the part and die are not identified (ml:dram:dram.org.part, unknown). (d) The source should cite Micron's Table 111 and Table 3 for tRFCab. g_trefi_max ('3.904 us') stays in the statement.

truth: The relay's pJ/B and its GB/s are per byte moved: each byte is counted once when it is written and again when it is read. The kernel reports stages × chunk × 2 bytes, the relay page calls it 'half a gigabyte of traffic' and '48 GB/s of reads and writes', and the reruns divide the energy by those bytes. A hand-off writes every byte once and reads it once, so one byte handed to the next shire costs 2 × 8.9 ≈ 17.8 pJ (≈232 pJ through DRAM). Per shire reached, the relay therefore costs about 17.8 pJ/B: about a sixth of a DRAM read (114.6), not a thirteenth, and no less than an L3 read over the mesh (14.7 [7.1-20.5]). The chart draws it as half that, below both. The 12.9-13.1× relay-vs-DRAM-relay ratio is unaffected. A sanity check gives the same answer: a DRAM tensor load plus a DRAM tensor store of one byte cost 132.6 + 141.9 pJ (random data), so 116.2 cannot be a write and a read together.

truth: In the measured relay (workloads/onchip, E25 and the V3 reruns), the hand-off medium 'reads the neighbour's scratchpad, write[s] your own'. Each stage tensor-stores its output into its own scratchpad, and the next shire pulls it with flw.ps vector loads from the previous shire's scratchpad. The data therefore cross the mesh as load replies, which go y first (L104). From shire 0 to shire 1 that route is 0 → 8 → 16 → 1, but the page draws the x-first request route 0 → 24 → 9 → 1 (and draws flow B's chain the same way). In the DRAM medium each shire writes and then reads back its own slot (the same address for the read and the write), so no next shire ever reads the DRAM copy. The numbers are unaffected; the mechanism and the drawn routes are wrong.

page_said: Fact: "The programmed timings are close to JEDEC LPDDR4's limits for a 16 Gb-per-channel die at 3,733 MT/s, as recalled from JESD209-4 and not checked against the standard: tRCD and tRPpb 18 ns minimum, tRAS 42 ns, tRRD 10 ns, tFAW 40 ns, tRFCab 280 ns; ..." Note: "tRFCab = 280 ns is the JEDEC value for 12-16 Gb per channel, a cross-check on the die density." Timeline panel: "An all-bank refresh every 3.875 µs, lasting 280.7 ns. Compared with JEDEC LPDDR4 as recalled, not checked against the standard (generic): the timings are close to its limits for this density and rate"
truth: JEDEC LPDDR4/LPDDR4X tRFCab depends on density per channel: 130 ns (2 Gb), 180 ns (3-4 Gb), 280 ns (6-8 Gb) and 380 ns (12-16 Gb). The card's DRAM is 16 Gb per channel (2 GB per channel; MR8 code 0110b), so JEDEC requires 380 ns. 280 ns is the JEDEC value for 6-8 Gb per channel, so it is no cross-check on a 16 Gb density; it points the other way. The firmware programs 280.7 ns (t_rfc_min = 262 DFI clocks), about 100 ns below JEDEC's minimum for this density. That is legal only because Micron rates its 16 Gb single-channel LPDDR4X die at an improved 280 ns, which its datasheet says supersedes the JEDEC value; the V3 card's DRAM is a Micron part. The other recalled limits are right, per the same datasheet's Table 196: tRCD and tRPpb 18 ns, tRAS 42 ns, tRRD 10 ns and tFAW 40 ns at 3,733 MT/s or below, RL 36 with DBI, WL 16 (set A), and tREFI 3.904 µs.

page_said: Parallel-prefix adders (Kogge-Stone, Sklansky, Brent-Kung) compute carries in log2(N) levels of generate/propagate cells.

where: Fact p.dopant.7 (kind: inference). It appears in the lib.channel panel and its parts, in lib.fin's 'gatestack' and 'thefin' parts (which show the channel panel), and in the p.dopant panel and its parts.
page_said: "The same patent dopes the wells under the fins at 10^16 to 10^18 per cm3. At those levels a 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm channel would hold on average 0.05 to 5.1 dopant atoms, among some 257,000 silicon atoms: a handful at most, and their random number and place would make every transistor different." (source: TSMC, US Patent 11,107,923 B2)
truth: The TSMC patent gives two well ranges. N-wells (P, As or Sb, implanted into the p-type region) are at most 1E18, 'such as between about 1E16 and about 1E18 atoms/cm3'. P-wells (B, BF2 or In, implanted into the NMOS region) are at most 1E20, 'such as ... between about 1E17 atoms/cm3 and about 1E20 atoms/cm3'. The wells 'may be formed in the fins and/or the substrate'. The NMOS that the page draws sits in a p-well, so the patent's range for it is 1e17-1e20, which is 0.5 to 515 atoms in this channel volume, not 0.05-5.1. The 1e16-1e18 range the arithmetic needs is the Berkeley TCAD study's fin doping (dope.levels). There is also a reference problem. In the lib.channel panel, p.dopant.3 (the fact that names the TSMC patent) is not listed, so 'The same patent' has nothing to refer to. In the p.dopant panel, the fact just before it (p.dopant.6) is sourced to IBM's patent.

where: Fact el.bus-bit. Its note is shown with the source on hover (ladder-panel.js:144) wherever the fact is listed (lib.flipflop, the lane and the wire panels).
page_said: Statement: "Toggling one operand-word bit outside the tensor unit costs 15.5 fJ: an effective 58 fF of wire and drivers at 0.517 V, about 190,000 electrons". Note: "Same E = C V^2 convention as et.flip-reg; a toggle that only discharges draws nothing from the supply, so this is an upper bound on C."
truth: A 0→1 toggle draws C·V² from the supply and a 1→0 toggle draws nothing, so the average toggle costs C·V²/2. 15.539 fJ per toggle therefore means C = 2E/V² = 116 fF (less any short-circuit energy). The 58 fF from E = C·V² is half of the physical switched capacitance, a low figure, not an upper bound. E = C·V² is right for et.flip-reg, where each clocking event is one full charge and discharge, but not for toggles. The 190,000 electrons (E/V = 30.1 fC drawn per toggle on average) is correct either way.

page_said: "In pure silicon electrons move about 3 times more easily than holes (mobility up to 1,400 vs 450 cm²/V·s); electrons saturate at about 8e6 cm/s, so crossing a 16.5 nm channel takes about 0.2 ps." (source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Electrical properties of Silicon (Si)")

The 8 x 10^6 cm/s is Hu's MOSFET-channel value (ch. 6). The research quoted Hu, but the displayed source omits him and the sentence calls it a property of 'pure silicon'. The transit time stays about 0.2 ps (0.16 ps at 1.0e7).
